notes.meaning: Paul opens his letter by identifying himself as an apostle, a messenger chosen and sent directly by Jesus Christ. He makes it clear that he did not appoint himself, but was called by the will of God. He also includes Sosthenes, a fellow Christian brother who was with him and known to the believers in Corinth.

Paul writes to the church gathered in Corinth, describing them as people made holy in Christ Jesus. Even though this congregation struggled with serious moral failures, they were still called saints because their standing rested on what Christ had done for them. He reminds them that they belong to a worldwide family of believers who call on Jesus as their Lord.

Paul gives a traditional Christian greeting of grace and peace. Grace is God's free, unearned kindness, and peace is the calm well-being that comes from being reconciled to God. Both blessings flow together from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul begins with heartfelt thanks to God for the believers in Corinth. He gives glory to God rather than praising human effort, because every blessing they received was a free gift through Jesus Christ. Even before addressing their problems, he thanks God for the genuine work of grace in their lives.

Christ had generously blessed the Corinthian church with spiritual wealth, especially in their speaking and knowledge. They could clearly share the message of faith and understood Christian truth deeply. Paul acknowledges these genuine abilities first, even though their pride in them would soon need correction.

The message about Christ had taken deep root and was proven true among them. God confirmed the truth of the gospel through the Holy Spirit's presence and the gifts active in their midst. Their changed lives showed that the message Paul brought was real.

Because of God's kindness, the believers in Corinth did not lack any spiritual gift needed for their Christian walk. As they used these gifts, they were eagerly waiting for the day when Jesus Christ will return in glory. Their present spiritual gifts were meant to encourage them as they looked forward to that final day.

differ.view: Pentecostal Christians emphasize that all spiritual gifts remain active and necessary for believers today while waiting for Christ's return.

notes.meaning: God promises to keep believers strong and steady until the end. When Jesus returns, they will stand before Him blameless, not because they never sinned, but because Christ's forgiveness covers them. Believers can take comfort knowing that their final protection comes from God.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand this to mean that God unconditionally guarantees every true believer will persevere in faith to the end.
Methodist Christians teach that God will keep believers secure on the condition that they remain faithful and keep trusting in Him.

notes.meaning: Believers can fully trust God because He is always true to His word. He is the one who called them into a shared life of close fellowship with His Son, Jesus Christ. Since God began this good work, He will reliably carry it through.

Paul moves from thanksgiving to a warm appeal for unity in the name and authority of Jesus Christ. He urges the believers to put away their rivalries and agree together in heart and purpose. His desire is to see them knit back together like a mended tear or a healed bone.

Paul explains why he has to correct them: members from Chloe's household brought him news about arguing in the church. Chloe was likely a Christian woman whose household members or workers traveled between Corinth and Ephesus. Paul brings the problem into the open because trustworthy witnesses had reported the strife.

Members of the church were forming rival groups based on their favorite leaders. Some favored Paul as the founder, others preferred the eloquent Apollos, some looked to Peter, and others proudly claimed only Christ to act superior to everyone else. Instead of focusing on the Lord, they were boasting in human teachers.

Paul asks three pointed questions to expose how foolish these divisions are. Christ cannot be carved up into pieces among competing factions. Paul did not die on the cross to save them, nor were they baptized into Paul's name, so all their loyalty belongs to Christ alone.

Paul is thankful that he personally baptized only a few people in Corinth, mentioning Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas. If he had baptized large numbers, people might have falsely claimed he was building a personal following. His casual aside that he did not remember baptizing anyone else shows that performing baptism was not his main task.

Paul explains that his primary mission from Christ was to preach the good news rather than to administer baptism. He deliberately avoided fancy language and clever human philosophy so the cross of Christ would not lose its power. Relying on polished human speech can easily distract people from the simple message that Jesus died for their sins.

The message that God saves people through a crucified Savior sounds like sheer nonsense to those who are on the path to destruction. But to those being saved, that same message is the mighty power of God bringing forgiveness and life. The cross divides all humanity into two groups based on how they respond to it.

Paul quotes Scripture from the prophet Isaiah to show that God has always planned to bring down human pride. Human intelligence on its own can never figure out how God saves sinners. God deliberately pushes aside worldly wisdom so that all the credit for salvation belongs to Him.

Paul challenges the smartest minds of his day, asking what the worldly wise, the Jewish legal scholars, and the Greek debaters have truly accomplished. None of their brilliant ideas could remove sin or bring people close to God. Through the cross, God proved that the world's wisdom is completely empty.

In God's wise plan, the world was never allowed to know Him through human philosophy alone. Instead, God was pleased to save those who trust in what the world mocks as a foolish message. Eternal life comes not through human cleverness, but through simple faith in Christ.

Paul points out what different cultures demanded before they would believe. Jewish listeners looked for miraculous signs from heaven to prove divine authority, while Greek listeners searched for intellectual systems and clever philosophy. Both groups wanted God to fit their own human expectations.

Rather than pleasing worldly tastes, the apostles simply preached that Jesus died on a cross for sinners. This message was a major stumbling block to Jewish hearers because the law taught that anyone hung on a tree was cursed by God. To Gentiles, relying on an executed man for salvation sounded completely ridiculous.

To those whom God calls, whether they come from Jewish or Greek backgrounds, Christ is the true answer to what they were searching for. In Him, they discover the genuine power of God that miracles alone could never give, and the deepest wisdom of God that human philosophy could never match. God opens their eyes to see that the cross is His greatest victory.

What the world calls God's foolishness is far wiser than the greatest human understanding, and what seems to be God's weakness is stronger than all human power. Christ's death looked like defeat, but it accomplished the greatest work on earth by overcoming sin and evil. God's ways always rise higher than human ability.

Paul tells the Corinthians to look at their own church family to see how God's kingdom operates. Very few of them were educated scholars, influential rulers, or born into wealthy and aristocratic families when God called them. God did not build His church by gathering the rich and famous elite.

God chose what the world looks down on as foolish, weak, and lowly to put human power and pride to shame. He used ordinary people whom society treated as nobodies to bring to nothing the things the world considers important. In this way, God reveals how little human status counts in His kingdom.

God chose this way of saving people so that no human being could ever boast in His presence. If salvation depended on human wealth, pedigree, or smarts, people would take credit for it. Because God saves people purely by His grace, all human boasting is taken away.

Believers are united with Christ Jesus entirely because of God the Father, not because of their own efforts. Christ has become true wisdom for us: our righteousness, meaning we are declared right with God; our holiness, meaning we are set apart to live for Him; and our redemption, meaning we are set free from sin. Everything needed for salvation is found in Jesus alone.

Paul concludes by quoting the prophet Jeremiah to show where all praise belongs. Since salvation is completely God's gift, anyone who wants to boast should boast only in the Lord. Believers find their true confidence and joy in knowing what God has done, not in what they have done themselves.
